Title: [2025] 3 S.C.R. 341 : 2025 INSC 306, The State of Goa & Anr. v. Namita Tripathi
Facts: An inspection conducted on 20.05.2019 in the premises of the respondent, a Professional Laundry Service, found violations of the Factories Act, 1948, including not possessing factory approved plans, using the premises as a factory without a valid factory licence, and not submitting any application for registration and grant of licence. full_details.Case Title & Citation: [2025] 3 S.C.R. 341 : 2025 INSC 306, The State of Goa & Anr. v. Namita Tripathi
full_details.Bench / Court: Supreme Court of India, Bench of B.R. Gavai and K.V. Viswanathan, JJ.
full_details.Facts of the Case: An inspection conducted on 20.05.2019 in the premises of the respondent, a Professional Laundry Service, found violations of the Factories Act, 1948, including not possessing factory approved plans, using the premises as a factory without a valid factory licence, and not submitting any application for registration and grant of licence. More than 9 workers were employed, and the manufacturing process of cleaning and washing of clothes was carried on.
full_details.Issues Framed: Was the High Court justified in quashing the process issued by the JMFC to the respondent for alleged violations of the Factories Act, 1948?
full_details.Arguments by Parties: The appellants argued that the respondent violated the Factories Act, 1948 by operating a laundry service without the necessary approvals and licences. The respondent contended that the activities carried out, including dry cleaning, did not constitute a 'manufacturing process' under the Act.
full_details.Court's Analysis / Reasoning: The Court held that the activities of washing, cleaning, and dry cleaning carried out by the respondent are covered under the definition of 'manufacturing process' as per the Factories Act, 1948. It rejected the respondent's contention that dry cleaning does not make any product usable, saleable, or worthy of transport, delivery, or disposal. The Court found that the premises in question operated as a 'factory' under the Act, and thus, the complaint and the order issuing process should not have been quashed.
full_details.Final Decision (Ratio Decidendi): The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, reinstated the complaint and the order issuing process of 04.12.2019, and held that the respondent's premises are indeed a 'factory' under the Factories Act, 1948, thus requiring the necessary licences and approvals.
